artifacts.summary: Verifies all cited file:line evidence, maps every handoff writer/reader across core/cslib/lean, evaluates candidate identity mechanisms against a still-live predecessor, resolves the Defect B session_id/cycle_count crux (per-task cumulative budget, explicit-override fix rather than a staleness signal or session_id gate), assesses defects 5 and 6, and proposes a shared report-vs-termination pattern file.

memory_candidates.content: In this repo's orchestrator engines, session_id is minted exactly once per /orchestrate command invocation (common_session_id() at GATE IN) and never regenerated mid-run, so a persisted-file's session_id mismatch is a fully reliable 'this is a different invocation' signal. Despite that reliability, scripts/test-session-runtime-files.sh Case 3 forbids gating cycle_count resets on it, because the loop guard is deliberately a per-task, cross-invocation cumulative budget -- gating on session_id would let an operator bypass MAX_CYCLES by simply re-invoking. When a budget/guard is meant to survive re-invocation by design, a reliable new-invocation signal is still the wrong lever to reset it; the correct fix for genuine exhaustion is an explicit, operator-typed override, not an automatic detector tied to invocation identity.

A staleness/freshness gate based only on file mtime (mtime < dispatch_start_ts) cannot detect a 'late writer' hazard where a predecessor process wakes and writes AFTER a successor's window opened -- that write has a NEWER mtime than the window start, so it passes the gate meant to catch only OLD (e.g. git-restored) files. Any single-slot shared-state file written by a process that can resume after reporting needs a content-embedded, orchestrator-minted identity (e.g. a monotonic dispatch_seq unknown to the predecessor in advance) rather than relying on timestamp comparison alone.
